newsitem.title: USA: ADM growth seen continuing despite probe.
newsitem.headline: ADM growth seen continuing despite probe.

text.p: A federal price-fixing probe over the past four years failed to stall Archer Daniels Midland Co's aggressive growth in the grain industry.
And despite a $100 million agreement Monday with the U.S. Justice Department that ended the investigation, ADM will continue to expand, grain analysts said.
"I think the direction of this company is pretty well outlined," said Leonard Teitelbaum, managing director of Merrill Lynch. "This should not change the direction of the company."

A federal court on Tuesday accepted ADM's guilty pleas to two counts of pricing-fixing in lysine, a feed additive, and citric acid, which is used in foods and beverages. The $70 million fine for lysine and $30 million fine for citric acid set records for U.S. Justice Department price-fixing actions.

Jim Quinton, a veteran grain merchandiser and market adviser, said he expects no change in ADM's activity in the market. ADM is among the most active players in the cash grain market to feed its ever-expanding demand.

"In terms of the (cash) market, I don't think it's going to change anything," Quinton said. "ADM will still process more and more bushels every year. They'll still buy out companies. This means life goes on as normal."
Even as federal investigators were sifting through ADM documents, the company continued to expand.
Since January 1996, ADM has signed deals to buy two U.S. grain companies, formed joint ventures with two foreign firms, and agreed to operate 20 grain facilities for a U.S. grain cooperative.

These deals included a letter of intent to buy Benson-Quinn Co, a Minneapolis-based grain merchandiser, and joint ventures with France's Rhone-Poulenc Animal Nutrition and with Countrymark Cooperative Inc, an Indianapolis-based cooperative.
ADM also bought a 22 percent share of Mexican corn flour giant Gruma SA and signed a letter of intent to buy Demeter Inc, an Indiana grain merchandising company.

Teitelbaum said future acquisitions would likely focus on international links and on firms that would augment ADM's livestock feed business, either in procuring raw materials or merchandising finished products.

ADM's expansion underscores its strategy to control its supply and costs of raw materials, such as corn and soybeans. By entering into joint ventures with cooperatives, such as Countrymark, ADM secures grain supplies directly from farmers.
ADM's accelerated expansion has raised a few eyebrows about consolidation in the grain-merchandising industry.
"What is ADM going to take over next?" one Ohio grain merchandiser quipped recently.

Despite ADM's growth, which has increased its reach particularly in the eastern Corn Belt, farmers are not wary of dealing with the agribusiness giant, according to Joe Miller, a market analyst at the Indiana Farm Bureau.

"I think ADM is perceived as being big, and any time a company gets to that size people start to become more cautious about what the company is doing," Miller said. "ADM has a fairly good name throughout the state (Indiana). I don't think there's anything negative about it."
ADM's main business ventures include oilseed processing and corn and wheat milling. It also operates barge, rail car and truck fleets and produces its own electricity to support its grain operations.
